extracted.intended_audience: orators, rhetoricians, and writers studying prose style (students of classical rhetoric)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing harmonious, agreeable prose: how to arrange words, choose forms, use cadence (prosaic numbers), and balance sound with sense to please the ear without sacrificing substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure — agreeable connection of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Our words should be so disposed that every following one may be aptly connected with the preceding, so as to make an agreeable sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to the structure of language so there is neither a chasm nor a disagreeable harshness; a moderate share of practice will habituate one to what is necessary. Avoid laborious nicety in minute exactness (ridiculed by Lucilius), but do ensure smooth linkage so the ear/mind readily discerns what ought to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concinnity / Sound — prefer words that please the ear
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere form and concinnity of our language should give our sentences their proper measure and dimensions; choose words principally for their agreeable sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer words that sound agreeable (not necessarily exquisitely melodious like poets' diction) and avoid flat or unmusical endings. Example contrasts: 'Auratos aries Colchorum' (moderate harmony) vs. 'Frugifera et ferta arva Alfiae tenet' (unmusical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cadence and Periods — numerous and measured cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods should have a numerous and measured cadence; a well-adjusted, full-measured flow of words gratifies the ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ear expects sentences to be properly tuned and measured; happy periods can elicit applause. Use complete and well-proportioned periods rather than broken, limping sentences; tune the compass of words to the compass of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of harsh phonetic collisions (e.g., vowel collision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid jarring collisions of vowels and other sounds that offend the ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romans generally avoid vowel collisions (some Greek authors allowed them). Example: prefer 'nobiscum' to 'cum nobis' because 'm' + 'n' would jar. Attention to such phonetic collisions improves euphony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of customary contractions and elisions for euphony
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract and abbreviate words where custom and ear prefer it (e.g., multi' modis, dein' for deinde), rather than insisting on full classical forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom oftentimes sanctifies such licences; contractions may be used to give a smoother sound. Examples: 'Duellum' → 'Bellum', 'axilla' → 'ala', 'nolle' for 'non velle'. Beware pedants who object to customary forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of strict etymology to the ear
rubrics_metrics.description: Etymological strictness may be sacrificed when the ear demands a different form; the ear's judgement should often prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alter letters or quantities to improve sweetness of language (examples: 'pomeridianas' vs 'postmeridianas', 'mehercule' vs 'mehercules'). The ear decides what is agreeable even if etymology would condemn it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment of syllable quantity and phonetic shape for harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: Change natural quantity or letter shapes in compounds to suit the ear (shorten/lengthen syllables as euphony requires).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: first syllable short in 'inclytus' and 'inhumanus' but long in 'insanus' and 'infelix'. Such liberties may be condemned by etymology but approved by sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition devices (succession, repetition, parallelism) to create concinnity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use particular forms—succession of similar terminations, parallel verbs, and repeating structures—to produce a measured cadence and apparent spontaneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tricolon/parallelism in 'didicimus, accepimus, legimus' or 'arripuimus, hausimus, expressimus'; antithesis examples ('Eam, quam nihil accusas, damnas'). Such forms should seem to arise naturally from sense rather than appear forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Antithesis and Contrast to generate rhetorical metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrasting similar and opposing circumstances (antithesis) will naturally produce rhetorical metre and measured sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antithesis can yield verse-like cadence in prose; examples include 'Bene quam meritam esse autumas, dicis male mereri' and other contrasted lines that end in a measured cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosaic numbers / measured prose (use of metre-like arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose can and should employ 'numbers' (prosaic metre) to harmonize and smooth the flow—these numbers correspond to metrical feet (dactyl, iambus, paeon) and their arrangement produces a numerous style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether and which metrical patterns to use; numbers should occur promiscuously. The author argues prose numbers are real and may be derived from poetic feet; their moderate use enriches oratory. Examples & historical attributions: Gorgias, Isocrates, Thrasymachus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation — avoid excessive artifice or slavish imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use measured style moderately; avoid over-exact attention to numbers that makes prose seem varnished or artificial and does not mask poor matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess (e.g., Gorgias' overuse) is offensive; prefer the moderate composed numbers of Isocrates. If the matter is good and words expressive, measured periods are appropriate; if not, metre merely varnishes emptiness and is censurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of reason (rules) and sensation (ear)
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing matter and word-sound, reason should govern informative choices and sensation (the ear) should govern pleasurable sound choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason determines rules of art for information; mere sensation governs the harmony intended for pleasure. Apply both: judgment for matter, ear for sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt the compass of language to thought — avoid defect and redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences should be neither defective nor redundant; adjust length and flow so the period pursues its course to a natural pause and matches the weight of the thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ear/mind perceives when a period is defective, mutilated, or immoderately long; in drama an audience will notice even a single misplaced syllable. Aim for completeness, proportion, and proper ending of periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural-sounding arrangements that seem unstudied
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of expression that produce regular turn and cadence should appear to result naturally from sense, not to be manifestly studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical figures so that 'the regular turn of them does not appear to have been studied, but to result entirely from the sense' — this increases perceived sincerity and force.
